My calls, then the truth — A knight/BISHOP wrong, B rook/ROOK, C rook/ROOK, D bishop/KNIGHT wrong, E king/KING, F queen/BISHOP wrong, G bishop/KNIGHT wrong, H queen/QUEEN. 4 of 8 squares, 3 of 6 types (rook, king, queen). Both bishops and both knights were called wrong, and I called the two rooks correctly only because they were the darkest and least featured crops — process of elimination, not because I saw a tower. Every crop reads as a bright circular plinth top with a small dark smudge standing on it.

Measured lit-glyph extent 13-18 px against the design's 0.38 m cap, which projects to 16.2 px at the near end. File letters at BLACK's end are complete on frame (cap line y=24.1, baseline y=9.0) but I needed 3.2x zoom and a gamma lift to read them confidently, and two of the eight are lost behind Black's plinths and a kerb fire. File letters at WHITE'S OWN end are CUT OFF in the 1920x804 judged capture: projecting the glyph box at |z| 10.06 to 10.50 gives cap line y=792.5-795.6 and baseline y=811.3-814.4 on an 804 px frame, so only 39-56% of each capital survives (a-file 56%, h-file 39%) and every baseline sits 7.3-10.4 px BELOW the last visible row. The comment in src/board/coords.ts claiming 'its baseline is 1.6 px short of the bottom of the play frame' is measurably wrong by 7 to 10 px. HONEST CAVEAT, and it matters: this clipping is an artifact of the capture harness's 2.388:1 frame, not of the play view. In a real 1280x640 browser window the near letters are complete and readable — I have the crop, and it reads H G F E D C B A. So on an actual desktop the coordinates are all there; it is only the frame this round is judged in that loses White's own file letters. They are small either way, about 9 px of cap at 1280x640. Three squares named from the picture alone: c5, f3, b6 — verified against the projection at (1089,345), (816,526), (1176,257), all three correct. Qualification: I read the RANKS off the numerals and COUNTED the files by position, because at 1:1 the letters need a zoom.

play: 8 moves clicked through the real canvas at 1280x640, no scripted path — every square projected through the app's own live camera and driven with mouse.click on the canvas. Line: 1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 Qxd4 5.Nf3 Qxd1+ 6.Kxd1 Bg4 7.Bc4 O-O-O+ 8.Bd2 Bxf3+, ending at 2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/8/2B5/2N2b2/PPPB1PPP/R2K3R w. All 8 accepted, no page errors. Every position was replayed through a FRESH Engine: legalMoves 30/38/36/38/2/28/6/5, each greater than zero, inCheck correctly true at plies 5, 7 and 8, and every FEN reachable from its predecessor by a legal sequence — ALL POSITIONS LEGAL AND REACHABLE. The line exercised a queen trade, a king recapture out of check, and Black castling long into check. ONE HONEST NOTE, AND I AM NOT BANKING IT AS A FINDING: I precomputed the engine's answers offline at the same 120,000-node budget and plies 1-7 reproduced move for move, but ply 8 diverged — offline predicted 8...Ne5, the live worker played 8...Bxf3+. I checked before blaming the engine, and I should not: another agent wrote src/game/interactive.ts at 09:10:59, which is inside the window in which plies 7 and 8 were played (roughly 09:05 to 09:15), so Vite will have hot-reloaded the interaction layer mid-game. The divergence is most likely that edit, not nondeterminism, and I am recording it as unresolved rather than as a defect. Nothing here touches the frozen capture path, which is separately proven byte-identical. For the record on provenance: src/pieces/device.ts (06:54) and src/pieces/index.ts (06:36) both predate my play-identity capture at 07:26, so every identifiability number in this critique is measured against the pieces tree as it stands. HONESTLY, COULD I CHOOSE BY LOOKING? Moves 1-3 yes, genuinely: I could see rank 2 was a solid row of men and ranks 3-4 empty, so I pushed a pawn two; and on move 3 I could see a dark man standing one square diagonally in front of my bright pawn, so I took it. Moves 4-8 no. From move 4 on I was choosing from memory of the starting layout, not from the picture, because I could not tell which back-rank man was a knight and which was a bishop — the same failure the crop metric measures. What rescued it is not the pieces: clicking a man paints small soft orange roundels on its legal destinations (I clicked g1 and got exactly three, on e2, f3 and h3, about 5-6 px across). They sit in a field of orange kerb fires but the fires are elongated streaks and these are round dots, so they are findable. That is the only reason a player who cannot name the pieces can still play.
biggestGap: The device collar works and the CAMERA throws it away: because the play camera sits on the board's centre line at 80 degrees, the two men of every same-type pair are rendered as horizontal MIRROR IMAGES of each other, and that parallax difference is larger than the difference between the six devices. Isolating the collar annulus (r 24-40 px, masking out the figure) makes the measurement WORSE than the whole crop — same 1.1112 vs different 0.9293, ratio 1.196, the most inverted region in the frame — but horizontally flipping the crops of the four men standing on the far side of the centre line flips that same annulus to same 0.6266 vs different 0.8722, ratio 0.718, the BEST number measured all round. The pockets are cut correctly and they are type-distinct; they simply land at mirrored screen positions, because a man at world +8.2 m and his twin at -8.2 m are seen from opposite sides. The mechanism in numbers: a chessman's full 0.85 m of height displaces its top by only 3.9 to 10.7 px against a 94.6 px file pitch, and that displacement is signed and antisymmetric about the centre line — a1 +9.9 px, h1 -10.0 px, b1 +7.0, g1 -7.1, c1 +4.2, f1 -4.2. Same-type MAD tracks that separation almost exactly: bishops at +-4.2 px score 0.667, rooks at +-9.9 px score 1.007, knights at +-7.1 px score 1.175. Nothing carved into the top of a plinth can beat this while the same object photographs differently depending on which half of the board it stands on.
critiqueDetail:
WHAT IS GENUINELY BETTER, said plainly. The devices in device.ts are real, they are on screen, and they are the right idea — counted pockets on the collar rim, nought/four/one/two/eight/five at four radii, cut from the same stone and shaded by the same Weather machinery. The reasoning in that file about pockets rather than bosses is correct as far as it goes, and the proof that it is correct is the mirror-corrected annulus number: 0.6266 same against 0.8722 different, which is a clean, large, correctly-signed separation from the collar ALONE with the figure masked out. The exposure complaint is also properly answered — fracBlown 0.00084 whole frame, 0.00000 in the board centre, medianLuminance 0.1216, histogramEntropy 6.574, coolFraction 0.8106 and meanLitHueDeg 213.8, detailTotal 0.02744. I am deliberately NOT quoting those as deltas against round 4's 0.051 / 5.656 / 0.0848 / 22.2 / 0.00508, because round 4 measured the knight-looking-up FILM shot and this measures the PLAY view — different camera, different lighting, different subject, so the comparison would be dishonest. What I can say against this frame on its own terms is that it is well exposed, correctly cool, and not clipped. This is a different and much better piece of work than the one I critiqued last time.

WHY IT STILL FAILS THE ROUND'S OWN TEST. device.ts anticipates the mirroring in one sentence — 'the two men of a type stand at MIRRORED files, so the same boss is lit from opposite hands on the two of them' — and answers it by making the device an occlusion cue, on the grounds that 'occlusion has no direction'. That is true of the SHADING and false of the GEOMETRY. Occlusion has no direction but a pocket still has a POSITION, and a pocket at world +x projects to the mirror of the same pocket at -x. At 30 m with a 38 degree vertical over 1920 px, a man standing 8.2 m off the centre line is seen obliquely enough that you look into the near inner wall of his collar and not the far one; his twin on the other side shows you the opposite wall. That is 10 px of parallax across a collar whose radius is about 40 px — a quarter of the whole device — and it is bigger than the difference between four pockets and eight.

I ran the obvious control before making this the headline, because the mirror flip also silently corrects a centring error: the plinth top stands above the board plane, so its projected centre is offset from the square's centre by the same signed lean, and flipping the crop fixes that too. Centring the annulus on the plinth top INSTEAD of the square centre, with no mirror correction, moves the ratio from 1.196 to 1.056 — better, but still inverted. Adding the mirror correction on top of correct centring takes it to 0.784. So the centring error is real and worth a little; the MIRROR is what actually flips the sign, and the claim survives its control.

The evidence is a ladder and every rung agrees. Whole 80x80 crop raw: 0.9499 / 0.8818, inverted. Collar annulus raw: 1.1112 / 0.9293, more inverted. Whole crop mirror-corrected: 0.5572 / 0.8359, correct. Collar annulus mirror-corrected: 0.6266 / 0.8722, correct. Piece-centred 48 px crop mirror-corrected: 0.7302 / 1.0416, correct. The information is there in every one of those masks; the projection is what is scrambling it. Re-centring the crop on the piece body instead of the square centre gets the raw number to 0.9019 / 0.9115, which is the only raw framing that is not inverted, and that is just the same effect seen from the other side — it removes about half the lean.

A SECOND FINDING, UNRELATED AND UNREPORTED ANYWHERE IN THE SOURCE: THE BOARD IS MIRRORED LEFT TO RIGHT. src/chess/index.ts states file 0..7 = a..h; layout puts file f at world x = (f-3.5)*2.35; and the play camera projects file a to screen x 1286.8 and file h to screen x 622.9 on a 1920 px frame, with the pale army at the bottom. So with White at the bottom of the screen, the a-file is on the player's RIGHT and h is on the LEFT. Four independent confirmations. (1) The projection, run through the app's own live camera. (2) The rendered inscription itself, which reads H G F E D C B A left to right — along the far kerb in the capture, and along WHITE'S OWN NEAR KERB in a 1280x640 window, where the letters are complete; no arithmetic of mine involved in either. (3) The app's own hit test: I clicked at screen x 606, left of a 1280 px frame's centre, and the game recorded the move as e2e4, which places the e-file left of centre when on a real board it is right of centre. (4) Pixels alone, using no file naming at all: the screen-leftmost square of rank 4 measures 0.170 (dark) and the screen-rightmost 0.665 (light), whereas a board seen from White's seat must have its leftmost rank-4 square light. The square COLOURS are correct — a4 is light and h4 dark, exactly as the rule requires — so this is purely a handedness error in how the board is presented, not a setup error. Its cost to a desktop player is total: the near-right corner is a1, a dark square, where every chess book says a player's near-right corner is h1 and light; and every coordinate read off the carved marks is left-right reversed against notation, diagrams and the game's own SAN record panel.

HONEST CORRECTION TO MY OWN METHOD, recorded because it nearly became a false finding. My first interactive driver read frames with canvas.toDataURL(), which in interactive mode returns an unpreserved WebGL drawing buffer; it handed back a stale start-position frame and I briefly believed the render was not tracking the engine. It is. Re-reading through a CDP compositor screenshot shows the board correct after every move, with the pawns gone from d2/e2, the black knight on c6 and a HUD carrying BLACK/THE ENGINE, WHITE/YOU and a SAN record reading '1. e4 Nc6 / 2. d4 d5'. No desync exists. I am flagging the tool bug rather than the app.

WHAT SAVES PLAYABILITY DESPITE ALL OF THIS, and it should be credited. Selecting a man paints small soft orange roundels on its legal destinations — I clicked g1 and got exactly three, on e2, f3 and h3. They are about 5-6 px across and they sit in a field of orange kerb fires, but the fires are elongated streaks and these are round, so they are findable. That is the only reason I could keep playing after the opening: I could not tell what any back-rank man was, but I could click one and read its dots.

ONE UNAMBIGUOUS NEXT MOVE. Make a man's appearance independent of which half of the board he stands on. The cheapest version is to stop projecting the collar under parallax: either render the play view orthographically from directly overhead, so a device at +8.2 m and the same device at -8.2 m produce identical pixels, or keep the perspective and make the device radially symmetric in COUNT rather than in placement — a ring of N identical pockets read as a count, which survives a mirror, instead of a pattern read as a shape, which does not. Target: the collar annulus at r 24-40 px must reach same < different WITHOUT the mirror correction. It is already at 0.6266 / 0.8722 with it, so the carving is done and only the projection is left.

history.gap: The pieces have no figurative geometry at all — every foreground chessman is a featureless tapered low-poly cone with visible flat-shaded facets, where the film frame shows armoured riders on rearing horses with cross-slit conical helms and curved sabres, crouching domed-helm pawns, and a huge draped chainmail cape, each on a hexagonal stepped moulded plinth.

The chessmen have silhouettes now but no SKIN: the pale army is uniform clean cold white with none of the film's irregular rust-ochre blotching, and every helm, torso, cape and shield is a smooth unbroken surface with zero carved incident (brow ridges, mail rings, shield rims and bosses, tabard/drapery folds, tooled chisel texture) — so mid-band detail sits at 0.0061 against the film's 0.0222, and each piece reads as an unfinished clay maquette rather than carved, stained limestone.

The pale army has grain now but still no PIGMENT: its stone carries zero rust-ochre staining, so where the film's limestone mottles from cool grey right up into warm rust — pale-stone warm/cool balance running p50 -0.13 to a p95 of +0.03, spread 0.26-0.31 — our pale pawns sit at p50 -0.287 with a p95 of -0.185, never once reaching even neutral. Every pale piece and plinth in the film is blotched over a third of its surface with hard-edged irregular orange-brown patches that pool in the mouldings and streak down the plinth steps; ours are uniform clean blue-grey stone from helm to base.

The device collar works and the CAMERA throws it away: because the play camera sits on the board's centre line at 80 degrees, the two men of every same-type pair render as horizontal MIRROR IMAGES of each other, and that parallax difference is larger than the difference between the six devices. The collar annulus alone (r 24-40 px, figure masked out) measures same 1.1112 vs different 0.9293 raw — the most inverted region in the frame — but horizontally flipping the four men on the far side of the centre line turns the same annulus into same 0.6266 vs different 0.8722, the best number measured all round. So the pockets are cut correctly and are type-distinct; they simply land at mirrored screen positions, because a man's 0.85 m of height displaces his top by only 3.9-10.7 px against a 94.6 px file pitch and that displacement is signed about the centre line (a1 +9.9, h1 -10.0). Whole-crop spec test 0.9499 same vs 0.8818 different, still inverted; blind human read 3 of 6 types.
